newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EP to condemn delay of EU ban on animal testing.
newsitem.headline: EP to condemn delay of EU ban on animal testing.

text.p: The European Parliament is expected next month to slam the European Union for trying to delay a planned ban on cosmetics tests on animals.
The EU approved a directive in 1993 ordering member states to end the sale of all cosmetics tested on animals by 1998.

But the Commission has now said it wants to delay the introduction of the directive until the year 2000 on the grounds that there has not been enough progress in developing internationally accepted alternatives to animal testing.

The Commission has warned that unless alternatives are suitably validated, exports of European cosmetics tested in this way may not be given legal approval in other countries, such as the United States.
It has also warned a blanket ban could face a challenge through the World Trade Organsation from cosmetic companies in countries like Japan and the U.S.
WTO rules allow the EU to outlaw animal-tested cosmetics manufactured domestically but not imports from third countries.

Euro-MPs are expected to adopt on March 14 a critical report by German Socialist Dagmar Roth-Behrendt which accuses the Commission of not pushing the cosmetics industry into finding new testing methods.

"Full implementation of the ban...will provide the greatest incentive for the industry, member states and the Commission to complete the necessary development of...non-animal alternative tests," says the draft report.
"We are very concerned about the delay," the Euro-MP told Reuters.
She said she would demand a Commission commitment not to try and postpone the ban beyond the year 2000.
The dispute mirrors a furious row between parliament and the Commission over the latter's repeated postponement of a planned ban on imports of fur from animals caught in steel-jawed leghold traps.
The Commission has argued for a delay on the fur import ban to give it time to reach an agreement on more humane trapping standards with Canada, Russia and the U.S., which still use the traps.
Trade commissioner Sir Leon Brittan has warned introduction of the fur ban could trigger a trade dispute.
